blocks.text: Codominance can be defined as a condition in which both the alleles of a gene pair in a heterozygote are equally expressed.
Examples: ABO blood group system

In the ABO blood group system, the I A and I B alleles are codominant in producing the AB blood group phenotype, in which both A and B-type antigens are produced. The genes responsible for the ABO blood group are located in chromosome 9.
The presence of both I A and I B causes the expression of both, forming the AB blood group. HLA gene also shows co dominance

The given clinical scenario of a male with tall stature, long limbs, joint hypermobility, arachnodactyly, aortic root dilatation, and similar features in his father suggests Marfan’s syndrome, an autosomal dominant condition and gene FBN1 (fibrillin-1) on chromosome 15.
The true statement regarding autosomal dominant inheritance is that most proteins lead to reduced production of a gene product or give rise to a dysfunctional or inactive protein.
**Autosomal dominant inheritance:** Autosomal dominant disorders are manifested in the heterozygous state, so at least one parent of an index case is usually affected.

items.text: **Autosomal Dominant Inheritance, Mutation in the CFTR Gene (Option A):** Cystic fibrosis (CF) is inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene. (chromosome 7)
**X-linked Recessive Inheritance, Mutation in the GBA Gene (Option B):** Gaucher disease is not associated with X-linked inheritance; instead, it follows autosomal recessive inheritance.

**Autosomal Dominant Inheritance, Mutation in the HEXA Gene (Option C):** Tay-Sachs disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the HEXA gene, resulting in deficient activity of the enzyme β-hexosaminidase A.

blocks.text: Cause – Niemann–Pick disease is due to sphingomyelinase deficiency, leading to sphingomyelin accumulation.
Type A is a severe infantile form with extensive neurologic involvement, marked visceral accumulations of sphingomyelin, progressive wasting and early death within the first 3 years of life.
In contrast, patients with type B disease have organomegaly but generally no central nervous system involvement. Patients usually survive into adulthood.
Affected cells become enlarged, due to the distention of lysosomes with sphingomyelin and cholesterol, imparting foaminess to the cytoplasm.
Image: Niemann-Pick disease in the liver. The hepatocytes and Kupffer cells have a foamy, vacuolated appearance due to the deposition of lipids.
Electron microscopy confirms that the vacuoles are engorged secondary lysosomes called zebra bodies.
Image: Zebra bodies
The clinical manifestations in the patients point to Rett Syndrome. It has X-linked dominant inheritance.

X-linked dominant disorders affect both males and females. All fathers that are affected by an X-linked dominant disorder will have affected daughters but not affected sons. However, if the mother is also affected then sons will have a chance of being affected, depending on whether a dominant or recessive X chromosome is passed on.
When the son is affected, the mother will always be affected.
Examples of X-linked dominant disorders (Mnemonic: RAVI-C):
Factor IX deficiency, associated with Hemophilia B, is an X-linked recessive disorder that predominantly affects males, as evidenced by the family history.

**X-Linked Recessive:** The gene for Hemophilia B is located on the X chromosome. Males (XY) express the disorder if they inherit the affected X chromosome since they lack a second X for compensation.

Females (XX) can be carriers if they inherit one affected X chromosome, often showing no symptoms due to the normal allele on the other X. Affected males cannot pass the disorder to sons but can pass the affected X to daughters, making them carriers.
Hemophilia A and B is X linked recessive
Hemophilia C is autosomal recessive

**MELAS -Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes:** MELAS follows a unique non-Mendelian pattern of inheritance called maternal inheritance, as mitochondrial DNA is derived entirely from the ovum.

Affected mothers and daughters transmit the disease to both male and female children, whereas the affected sons don't transmit the affected DNA. (Mother to all, Father to none.) The most common mitochondrial disease is MELAS.
Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) affects the SNORP gene on chromosome 15q. PWS is due to paternal deletion and maternal imprinting of the given gene. Subset of PWS can also occur due to maternal disomy

blocks.text: The below-mentioned disorders are trinucleotide repeat disorders where there is excessive repetition of trinucleotides.
In Introns/ Non coding region:
In Exons/ Coding region: Huntington's disease - CAG (Mnemonic- Hunter in a Cage)

HD is a CAG trinucleotide repeat disorder, seen in the axon region of a gene present on chromosome 4. HD is characterised by the Anticipation/Sherman Paradox. The number of repeats increases with every generation, leading to early and more severe presentation in the next generation.
HD features psychiatric disturbances and choreoathetosis early on, with cognitive disturbance and death later.

blocks.text: A single mutant gene leading to many end effects is called pleiotropism, whereas mutations at several genetic loci producing a similar phenotypic effect are called genetic heterogeneity.
Sickle cell anemia is an example of pleiotropy with a single gene mutation causing multiple physical effects: Mutation at beta-7 position: Glutamic acid is replaced by valine.
The mutation produces hemoglobin S (HbS), which makes red blood cells prone to hemolysis. Additionally, it can lead to complications like splenic fibrosis, organ infarcts, and bone pains.
